name: Cuttlefish
description: 10 million chromatophores create passing-wave displays that hypnotize prey. W-shaped pupil admits light from all directions. Can display two different patterns on left and right body halves simultaneously. Cuttlebone buoyancy precision-tuned by gas diffusion.

core_attributes.neurology: chromatophore motor cortex, W-pupil optical system, split-brain display
core_attributes.pattern: hypnotic wave displays, instant chromatophore adaptation, split-bilateral camouflage

scope.definition: Prey capture success rate when cuttlefish employ traveling chromatophore wave display (hypnotic pattern) immediately before strike, compared to 0.58 for non-display approach.

evidence.source: Hanlon & Messenger (2018) 'Cephalopod Behaviour', 3rd ed., Cambridge UP; Langridge (2009) 'Cuttlefish use startle displays but not against large predators', Animal Behaviour 77:847-856.
cross_domain_examples: traveling wave display during prey approach raises shrimp capture success from 0.58 to 0.91
passing cloud display toward predators: cuttlefish body pattern mimics moving shadow to confuse
mantis shrimp use UV signaling (invisible to most fish) for species communication — parallel covert channel

scope.falsifiability: If controlled removal of chromatophore wave display (via pigment-cell paralysis) shows no change in prey capture success, the hypnotic-disorientation hypothesis fails.
scope.measurement_limits: Display effectiveness is prey-species specific — most effective against crustaceans, less so against fish. Measurement requires split-plot design with same individual in display vs no-display conditions.

scope.definition: Time from visual detection of novel substrate to full pattern match — measured as latency (ms) and spectral similarity score (fraction of background reflectance spectrum matched) in substrate-change experiments.

evidence.source: Packard & Sanders (1971) 'Body patterns of Octopus vulgaris and maturation of the response', Animal Behaviour 19:780-790; Hanlon et al. (2009) dynamic camouflage in cephalopods.
cross_domain_examples: cuttlefish achieve 90% substrate spectral match within 200 ms of substrate change
chromatophore expansion: individual cells expand from 1 mm to 3 mm in <300 ms via direct neural control
flounder: fastest vertebrate camouflage at 1-2 s vs cuttlefish 200 ms — cephalopod advantage
metamaterial adaptive camouflage surfaces: engineered cephalopod-inspired color-change tiles (DARPA)

scope.falsifiability: If substrate-matching accuracy measured photometrically falls below 0.70 in controlled experiments, the near-perfect camouflage claim overstates spectral matching.
scope.measurement_limits: Cuttlefish are colorblind (monochromatic vision) but achieve color match via polarization and brightness patterns. Color matching measured by human/camera perception, not cuttlefish-eye perception.

scope.definition: Precision of cuttlebone gas-liquid ratio adjustment — standard deviation of vertical drift rate (m/hr) at neutral buoyancy, as fraction of neutral buoyancy target depth.

evidence.source: Denton & Gilpin-Brown (1961) 'The buoyancy of the cuttlefish', Journal of the Marine Biological Association UK 41:319-342; Ward & Boletzky (1984) shell buoyancy studies.
cross_domain_examples: cuttlebone maintains neutral buoyancy within ±5% of target depth via gas-liquid ratio adjustment
adjustment response time 2-4 hours for 10 m depth change — slower than swim bladder fish
submarine ballast tanks: engineered neutral buoyancy via gas-liquid ratio control — same principle

scope.falsifiability: If cuttlefish buoyancy drift exceeds ±15% of target depth in pressure-controlled experiments, the fine-control buoyancy model overstates precision.
scope.measurement_limits: Buoyancy control works best in the 0-200 m depth range for which cuttlebone evolved. Crushing depth is ~600 m. Rapid depth changes exceed adjustment rate and require active swimming compensation.
